{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01T9mM7MUwBRSWy7tqenkNbf","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# BUILD PLAN — output format\n2\t\n3\tEmit the plan in exactly these sections, in this order. Keep it concrete: name real\n4\ttechnologies and real checks, not placeholders. Length is not quality: prefer one-line table\n5\tcells, cite IDs (V2, Phase 3, E1) instead of restating content, and scale the plan to the system.\n6\tA section with nothing load-bearing is one line (\"None.\", \"N/A — <reason>\"); a section that a\n7\tdeclared exception makes moot is one line citing it.\n8\t\n9\t---\n10\t\n11\t## 1. Classification and constraints\n12\t- **What:** one line on the system.\n13\t- **Type:** software / infra / AI-agentic (or a mix); greenfield or brownfield; small build or not.\n14\t- **Dominant constraint:** correctness | availability | latency | cost | scale | compliance.\n15\t- **Worst failure:** the single failure that would hurt most.\n16\t\n17\t**Budgets** (only the rows that bind; add rows the system needs, such as a cutover freeze window):\n18\t\n19\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n20\t|---|---|---|---|\n21\t| Latency | … | REQUIREMENT / BASELINE / ASSUMPTION / UNKNOWN | V… or Phase … |\n22\t| Throughput | … | … | … |\n23\t| Availability / SLO | … | … | … |\n24\t| RPO / RTO | … | … | … |\n25\t| Resource use | … | … | … |\n26\t| AI inference cost | … (AI systems only) | … | … |\n27\t| Storage cost | … | … | … |\n28\t| Operational complexity | … (e.g. services to run, on-call load) | … | … |\n29\t\n30\tAn UNKNOWN target has no number: write the missing input, who supplies it, and the phase that\n31\tneeds it. An ASSUMPTION gives its basis.\n32\t\n33\t**Missing inputs:** the unknowns that would change the plan most, and any assumption the phase\n34\torder rests on.\n35\t\n36\t## 2. Dependency map\n37\tOnly the dependencies that bind and that the phase order does not already show:\n38\t\n39\t| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n40\t|---|---|---|---|\n41\t| … | … | decision / validation / risk-security / organizational / economic (structural or runtime only when surprising) | built / deployed / specified / hardened / exposed / committed |\n42\t\n43\tThen one line naming the kinds with no instance (\"No organizational or economic dependencies.\").\n44\tIn brownfield work, mark each dependency CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n45\t\n46\t## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n47\t\n48\t| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n49\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n50\t| Consistency vs availability | R2/R3 + one-clause reason | … | … | V…, a cheap check, or the cited basis | … (for a gated row: \"V… fails, or …\") |\n51\t| Monolith vs services | … | … | … | … | … |\n52\t| Sync vs async | … | … | … | … | … |\n53\t| Build vs buy | … | … | … | … | … |\n54\t| Data-privacy boundary (personal or regulated data) | … | … | … | … | … |\n55\t| <each system-specific R2/R3 decision, e.g. the tenancy model> | … | … | … | … | … |\n56\t| (Brownfield) migration strategy, coexistence and cutover, rollback, system of record | … | … | … | … | … |\n57\t| (AI) prompt+RAG vs fine-tune | … | … | … | … | … |\n58\t| (AI) hosted API vs self-host | … | … | … | … | … |\n59\t\n60\t**R1 defaults:** <decision> → <default>; … (one line; no rows for R1 decisions).\n61\t**N/A:** <considered decisions that do not apply> — <reason> (one line).\n62\tOmit the (Brownfield) and (AI) rows when they do not apply. Inherited brownfield decisions the\n63\tplan will not change are listed once as constraints, not as rows.\n64\t\n65\t## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n66\t- The one real request and the real response.\n67\t- Every tier it crosses.\n68\t- How it is deployed, logged, monitored, and rolled back on day zero.\n69\t- Who can reach it (internal or allow-listed traffic behind a flag until its controls exist).\n70\t\n71\tIf an exception changes Phase 0, say so in one line and cite it (E…).\n72\tExit check (V0): a real request succeeds with one trace across every tier; a deploy and a\n73\trollback succeed through the pipeline; an injected failure fires an alert; the first values of\n74\tthe measurable budgets are recorded as baselines, not targets.\n75\t\n76\t## 5. Phases (Phase 1 onward; dependency order; within a phase, rework widest first, exposure smallest first)\n77\tFor each phase:\n78\t- **Phase N — <name>**\n79\t  - Unlocks: what becomes possible after it.\n80\t  - Depends on: earlier phases and V-IDs, by reference.\n81\t  - Tasks: in order.\n82\t  - Rollback: how this phase is undone, or its point of no return and the gate that guards it.\n83\t  - Exit check: its gates pass, plus any observable condition that no gate covers.\n84\t\n85\t## 6. Validation gates\n86\t\n87\t| ID | Hypothesis | Method | Acceptance threshold | Evidence | Unlocks (and if it fails) | Phase |\n88\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n89\t| V0 | A change can be deployed, observed, and rolled back through every tier in production | … | the V0 exit check in §4 | … | Phase 1 | 0 |\n90\t| V1 | … | … | … (labeled) | the artifact it will produce and where it is kept | … ; if it fails: … | … |\n91\t\n92\tOne row per gate the plan cites, and no others. Every threshold carries its label. Evidence names\n93\tan artifact the check will produce, never a result. Phase may read \"starts in N, required before M\".\n94\t\n95\t## 7. Cross-cutting concerns (per phase, from the first commit)\n96\t\n97\t| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n98\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n99\t| 0 | … | … | … | … |\n100\t\n101\tObservability appears in Phase 0. No cell is empty; where a declared exception bypasses one, cite\n102\tit (E…).\n103\t\n104\t## 8. AI layer (AI/agentic systems only)\n105\t\n106\t| Sublayer | In this system | Built in | Exit check or V-ID |\n107\t|---|---|---|---|\n108\t| 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense | … | Phase … | … |\n109\t| 2. Cost + latency budget | … | … | … |\n110\t| 3. Human-in-the-loop gating | … | … | … |\n111\t| 4. Retrieval | … | … | … |\n112\t| 5. Model access | … | … | … |\n113\t| 6. Memory | … | … | … |\n114\t| 7. Orchestration | … | … | … |\n115\t| 8. Routing | … | … | … |\n116\t| 9. Feedback | … | … | … |\n117\t\n118\tA capability sublayer (4–9) this system does not need: \"Not needed — <reason>\". The defenses\n119\t(1–3) are always needed when the system takes untrusted input, spends money, or acts on the\n120\tworld. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01WyUiTswUM1YKqqbdLzXR9a","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n2\t\n3\tExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n102\t| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n103\t| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n104\t| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n105\t\n106\tNot exceptions:\n107\t\n108\t- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n109\t- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n110\t  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n111\t  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n112\t- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n113\t  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n114\t  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n115\t- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\nsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n\n## 1. Dependency kinds\n\n| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n\nCommon misses:\n\n- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n\n## 2. Validation gates\n\nFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n\n| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n\nShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\nso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n\nA good acceptance threshold:\n\n- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n  security, or legal judgment;\n- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n\nAnti-patterns:\n\n- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n  correct, or affordable enough.\n- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n  UNKNOWN has no number.\n- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n  sublayer.\n- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n\n## 3. Reversibility\n\n| Tier | Examples |\n|---|---|\n| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n\nCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\nbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\nundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\nirreversible operation.\n\nBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\nprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n\nSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\ninterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\nraw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\nthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\non every row from day one.\n\n## 4. Budgets\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n\nRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\nis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n\n## 5. Methodology exceptions\n\n| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n\nNot exceptions:\n\n- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n- Brownfield work. {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_khwl6u5ljou2l6iuhrgicnlmaraoshxn3ukl4bgtfeskcnreqkpa","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# Build plan: moving the hospital's patient scheduling system to the cloud with no downtime\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** Move the hospital's on-premises patient scheduling application and its database to a cloud account the hospital owns. Users, interfaces and outside vendors must keep working throughout.\n- **Type:** Infrastructure plus software. It replaces an existing system (brownfield). It's a large build: protected health information (PHI), clinical users, several teams and vendors, and some decisions that are hard to undo.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness of bookings during the move, then availability, then compliance.\n- **Worst failure:** Two databases accepting writes at once (split-brain), or a cutover or rollback that silently loses or duplicates appointments. Patients miss care or get double-booked, and nobody notices for days. The controls against it are V4, V5, V6 and fencing (only one database can ever accept writes), described in Phase 3.\n\n**Planning assumptions** (if any is false, the plan changes as noted):\n- The hospital runs the system itself on one relational database. The vendor supports running it on cloud servers. Users reach it through hostnames the hospital controls. **If false:** if the vendor's own hosted offering is the target, this becomes a vendor-led move and Phases 1–3 are re-planned around their tools. If desktop clients connect straight to the database, a database-name step is added to Phase 2.\n- **HIPAA applies (US).** If not, V1 is re-scoped to the local rules (for example GDPR or NHS DSPT) and the data-location row in §3 changes.\n- **The scheduling database is not shared with other applications** (for example registration). If it is, the move covers every application on it and Phase 2 grows.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Planned downtime during the move | None visible to users; reading schedules works throughout | REQUIREMENT (the request) | V5, V6 |\n| Pause in saving changes at switchover | ≤ 30 s; in-flight saves are retried, not failed | ASSUMPTION: fits inside normal app and client timeouts. Clinical operations must confirm a pause this short doesn't count as \"downtime\" (Phase 0 task) | V5 |\n| Booking data loss (RPO) | No saved booking lost, through cutover or rollback | ASSUMPTION: a lost booking can mean missed care; Chief Medical Information Officer (CMIO) to confirm | V4, V5 |\n| Time to roll back to on-premises (RTO) | ≤ 15 min | ASSUMPTION: keeps a rollback a short interruption, below the hospital's trigger for paper downtime procedures. Clinical operations to confirm against that trigger | V5 |\n| Speed of key actions (find slot, book, reschedule, cancel) | 95th-percentile time ≤ 1.1× today's | BASELINE measured in Phase 0; the 10% allowance is an ASSUMPTION | V3 |\n| Throughput | Handles 2× today's busiest hour | BASELINE measured in Phase 0; 2× headroom is an ASSUMPTION | V3 |\n| Replication delay (on-premises → cloud) | 99th percentile ≤ 5 s at peak | ASSUMPTION: lets the copy fully catch up inside the 30 s pause | V3, V4 |\n| HL7 interface messages | Zero lost or duplicated | ASSUMPTION: a duplicate scheduling message creates a duplicate appointment in the EHR | V5, V6 |\n| Ongoing availability | — | UNKNOWN: needs the service owner's committed target before Phase 3. The floor is \"no worse than BASELINE\", measured from Phase 0 | Phase 3 soak, Phase 4 |\n| Cloud running cost | — | UNKNOWN: Finance supplies the budget before Phase 1 sizing is committed | Phase 1 exit check, Phase 4 |\n| Running two environments at once | ≤ 90 days from the first patient data in the cloud to decommissioning | ASSUMPTION: one infrastructure team carrying both | Phase 4 |\n\n**Missing inputs, most important first:**\n1. Which product this is, and the vendor's written support and licensing terms for the cloud.\n2. Client type: web, or desktop clients connecting directly to the database.\n3. Database engine, version, size and peak volumes.\n4. Cloud provider, and whether a business associate agreement (BAA, the HIPAA contract with the provider) is already signed.\n5. Clinical operations' definition of \"no downtime\".\n6. Whether the database is shared with other applications.\n\n**Things this plan will not change (each with its cost to change):**\n- Application version: an upgrade means re-testing clinical workflows, which is weeks of work.\n- Database engine: changing it means rewriting the schema and stored code, which is months.\n- HL7 interfaces stay on the on-premises interface engine: re-pointing them affects every partner system.\n- Login stays on Active Directory (AD): changing the login model changes the security boundary.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Any PHI in the cloud (copying the database, the cloud test server) | BAA signed with the cloud provider; V1 | Organizational + security (CONFIRMED under HIPAA) | Exposed (Phase 0) |\n| Turning on replication from the live database; adding the cloud test server | Change advisory board (CAB) approval through the existing change process | Organizational (CONFIRMED) | Deployed (Phase 0) |\n| Full-volume replication, V3 and V4 | Two private circuits on separate paths (carrier lead time of weeks; a VPN is enough for Phase 0) | Organizational + runtime (ASSUMED) | Deployed (Phase 1) |\n| Cloud server sizing and licences | Vendor support statement and licence rights in the cloud; Finance's cost budget | Organizational + economic (ASSUMED) | Committed (Phase 1) |\n| Cloud app servers | AD domain controllers, DNS, time servers, print servers (appointment letters) and email relay reachable from the cloud | Runtime (ASSUMED; found by V2) | Deployed (Phase 1) |\n| Re-pointing consumers; the cutover runbook | V2: the full list of what depends on the system | Validation | Specified (Phase 2) |\n| Cutover thresholds (V5, V6) | Clinical operations' definition of \"no downtime\"; CMIO confirming no booking loss | Decision + organizational | Specified (Phase 0 task, needed by Phase 2) |\n| Outside vendors calling the app (SMS reminders, patient portal) | Their IP allow-list changes and change windows | Organizational (ASSUMED) | Exposed at cutover (Phase 3) |\n| Production cutover | V4, V5, V6; refreshed paper downtime procedures; staff on site | Security + organizational | Exposed (Phase 3) |\n| Decommissioning on-premises | V7; sign-off from records retention and legal | Organizational | Committed (Phase 4) |\n\nAll seven kinds of dependency apply here. The ordinary build dependencies are already covered by the phase order.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates\n\n| Decision | How hard to reverse | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | What would flip it |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Consistency vs availability | R3: a split-brain double-books patients, and that harm can't be undone | One database accepts writes at any moment; no two-way live writing. The switch uses a short pause in saving, with fencing | Users can tolerate a ≤ 30 s pause in saving | V5, V6 | V5 pause exceeds budget → switch over in an app-wide read-only mode with an on-screen banner, in the quietest window |\n| Migration approach | R2: weeks of re-planning | Move the app servers as-is; database on the same engine and version (managed only if it supports native replication; otherwise on a cloud server) | Vendor supports it; no database features block it | Phase 1 compatibility check + vendor statement | Vendor refuses, or a blocking feature turns up → database on a cloud server, same engine |\n| Replication: build vs buy | R2: swapping tools means re-copying the database | Use the database engine's own log-based replication, which also runs in reverse for rollback | Same engine and version on both sides | V4 | V4 finds differences, or native replication is impossible → a third-party change-capture tool with stricter reconciliation |\n| Which system is the official record, and how cutover works | R3: an hour wrong can lose or double bookings | On-premises stays the official record until V6. Then a single database switch, with reverse replication kept running through a 30-day soak | Reverse replication keeps pace | V5, V6 | Any rollback trigger in V6 fires → switch back to on-premises |\n| How consumers find the system | R2: changes coordinated across many teams | Every consumer (users, interfaces, vendors) uses stable hostnames behind a proxy the hospital controls. Cutover becomes a proxy change | Every consumer can be re-pointed | V2 | A consumer can't be re-pointed (hard-coded appliance) → an address-translation shim on-premises |\n| Data-privacy boundary | R3: exposed PHI can't be recalled | PHI only in a hospital-owned account, in-country region, BAA-covered services, private network only, hospital-managed encryption keys. Test environments use de-identified data. Logs and traces that contain identifiers are treated as PHI | Provider covers every service used | V1 | A service isn't BAA-covered, or a data-location rule rules out the region → a different service or region |\n| Network link to the cloud | R2: carrier lead time | Two private circuits on separate paths plus a backup VPN. After cutover, on-site scheduling depends on this link | Failover doesn't drop sessions | V5 (link-cut test) | Failover test fails → add a third path from a different carrier before V6 |\n| High availability and disaster recovery (DR) in the cloud | R2 | Synchronous copies across availability zones in one region. Until V7, the reverse-replicated on-premises copy is the DR. A second-region DR copy is required before decommissioning | Zone failover stays within budget | V5, V7 | Zone failover misses the RTO → re-plan the high-availability setup |\n\n**Low-stakes defaults (R1):** infrastructure code → Terraform; monitoring backend → extend the existing security log system (SIEM) and performance monitoring; build pipeline → the existing one.\n\n**Not applicable:**\n- Monolith vs services: no re-architecture during a move.\n- Sync vs async: inherited (HL7 stays asynchronous through the interface engine).\n- AI rows: no AI component.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\nThe skeleton is the thinnest real path through the new cloud setup, used by IT staff only, with the current system untouched as the fallback.\n\n- **The real request:**\n  1. An IT analyst on the allow-list books, then cancels, a slot for the hospital's designated test patient in a designated test clinic.\n  2. The booking is done through one cloud app server.\n  3. The booking is then read back from the cloud database copy.\n- **Path it takes:**\n  1. Hospital workstation → internal DNS and proxy, on a separate hostname.\n  2. Site-to-site VPN → private-only cloud load balancer → one cloud app server, running the same build as production.\n  3. On-premises live database (still the official record) → interface engine → EHR scheduling message for the test patient.\n  4. Native replication → cloud database copy → a check query confirms the booking arrived.\n- **Deploy, log, monitor, roll back:**\n  - The landing zone and the app server image deploy through the pipeline from Terraform.\n  - Logs and traces go to the SIEM, classified as PHI.\n  - Alerts go to the existing on-call: app health and replication delay.\n  - Rollback: take the server off the hostname, revert the infrastructure code, stop replication through the CAB plan, and destroy the cloud copy's encryption key so the copy can never be read again.\n- **Who can reach it:** only allow-listed IT workstations, on a separate internal hostname. Clinical users keep using the on-premises system unchanged. No outside access. No PHI goes into the cloud until V1 passes.\n- **Exit check (V0):**\n  - The test booking traces end to end through every tier.\n  - One deploy and one rollback run through the pipeline.\n  - A deliberately killed replication stream fires an alert.\n  - First baselines are recorded: speed of key actions, replication delay, and the extra delay of the app calling the database across the VPN. These are a floor at near-zero load, not capacity.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n**Phase 0 — Prerequisites, baselines and the skeleton**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 1.\n- **Depends on:** nothing earlier.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Start the long-lead-time items: CAB approval, BAA, cloud account, order both circuits, ask the vendor for its support and licensing statement, get clinical operations' definition of \"no downtime\" and the CMIO's confirmation on booking loss.\n  2. Measure today's live system through its own change process: automated test transactions for the key actions, the busiest hours, availability.\n  3. Start dependency discovery: network flow logs plus a database connection audit, covering at least 35 days including a month-end (V2).\n  4. Build the landing zone with Terraform: private-only network, hospital-managed keys, SIEM logging, sign-in with multi-factor authentication.\n  5. Pass V1.\n  6. Set up the VPN, seed the cloud database copy, deploy the app server.\n  7. Run V0.\n- **Rollback:** as described in §4. The live system's only change is replication being turned on, which can be turned off under the CAB plan.\n- **Exit check:** V1 and V0 pass; baselines recorded; discovery running.\n\n**Phase 1 — Production-scale data tier and proof the copy is identical**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 2.\n- **Depends on:** V0, V1, both circuits installed.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Compatibility check: vendor statement plus database features in use.\n  2. Size the cloud database and app tier across availability zones.\n  3. Move replication onto the circuits.\n  4. Start continuous reconciliation between the two databases (V4). It compares row counts and checksums only, never records.\n  5. Stand up in the cloud the runtime services discovery found: AD domain controllers, DNS, print servers, email relay.\n  6. Replay production load against the cloud stack (V3).\n  7. Test-restore a cloud backup.\n- **Rollback:** tear down the cloud tier. On-premises is still the official record and still serving everyone.\n- **Exit check:** V3 passes; V4 reconciliation running with alerts; cost estimate checked against Finance's budget.\n\n**Phase 2 — Re-point consumers, cut over read-only consumers first, rehearse**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 3.\n- **Depends on:** V2, V3, V4 running.\n- **Tasks** (smallest exposure first):\n  1. Move every consumer V2 found onto stable hostnames behind the hospital proxy, one consumer group at a time, still pointing at on-premises. Each move is undone with a DNS change.\n  2. Move read-only consumers (data warehouse loads, reports) onto the cloud copy.\n  3. Optional, only if V3 shows the cloud app calling the on-premises database across the link stays within budget: put one low-volume clinic's schedulers on cloud app servers for 1 week.\n  4. Script the cutover runbook.\n  5. Run V5 rehearsals.\n  6. Pre-stage outside vendors' allow-list changes.\n  7. Refresh paper downtime procedures and the printed 48-hour schedules.\n- **Rollback:** re-point each group or read-only consumer back by DNS or proxy.\n- **Exit check:**\n  - V2 and V5 pass.\n  - No traffic on the old addresses for 7 days.\n- **Note on exposure:** the write path can't be trialled with a small group without two databases accepting writes, which §3 rules out. Exposure is narrowed by sequence instead: IT staff, then read-only consumers, then one clinic, then the full switch.\n\n**Phase 3 — Production cutover and soak**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 4.\n- **Depends on:** V4 (14 days, plus the last 72 h clean), V5, V6.\n- **Tasks**, in the quietest window from the baseline (never just before a release of new booking slots):\n  1. The interface engine holds incoming HL7 messages.\n  2. Pause saving.\n  3. Wait until replication delay is zero.\n  4. Fence: demote the on-premises database to read-only and turn off the old app servers' database logins.\n  5. Promote the cloud database.\n  6. Switch the proxy and drain sessions.\n  7. Release the held HL7 messages.\n  8. Start reverse replication, cloud → on-premises.\n  9. Run booking integrity checks every 5 minutes.\n  10. Soak for 30 days including a month-end.\n- **Rollback:** the same script run in reverse back to on-premises, within the RTO, while reverse replication runs.\n- **Exit check:**\n  - V6 post-cutover criteria held for the whole soak.\n  - Availability at or above BASELINE.\n\n**Phase 4 — Steady state and decommissioning**\n- **Unlocks:** the end of running two environments.\n- **Depends on:** Phase 3 soak; V7.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Build a second-region DR copy and test a restore.\n  2. Make a final archive export and test that it restores.\n  3. Pass V7.\n  4. Stop reverse replication.\n  5. Decommission: wipe media to NIST 800-88, revoke credentials, remove firewall rules.\n- **Point of no return:** stopping reverse replication. V7 guards it.\n- **Exit check:** V7 passes; nothing still depends on the on-premises hosts.\n\n## 6. Validation gates\n\n| ID | Hypothesis | Method | Acceptance threshold | Evidence | Unlocks (and if it fails) | Phase |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| V0 | A change can be deployed, observed and rolled back through every tier in production | The skeleton in §4 | The V0 exit check in §4 | Trace ID, pipeline run records, alert record, baseline sheet in the migration repository | Phase 1; if it fails, fix the broken tier before anything else | 0 |\n| V1 | The cloud boundary is safe for PHI | BAA executed. HIPAA risk analysis updated. Configuration scan: no public endpoints, encryption at rest with hospital keys, encryption in transit, audit logs reaching the SIEM, least-privilege access, emergency access logged | Pass/fail sign-off from the CISO and the Privacy Officer | Signed BAA, updated risk analysis, scan report, sign-off record (compliance repository) | Copying PHI into the cloud (Phase 0 seed onward); if it fails, the skeleton runs on a de-identified copy and Phase 1 is blocked | 0 |\n| V2 | We know everything that depends on the system | Flow logs plus database connection audit, ≥ 35 days including a month-end; every flow traced to an owner | Zero unidentified connections; every consumer CONFIRMED, with its cutover action and owner sign-off | Inventory and owner sign-offs (CMDB) | Re-pointing consumers and the cutover runbook; if it fails, extend discovery and Phase 2 waits | Starts in 0, required before 2 |\n| V3 | The cloud stack is as fast as today's, and replication keeps up | Replay production load at 2× BASELINE peak for 4 h, including a simulated Monday-morning burst; also measure the app calling the database across the link | 95th-percentile key actions ≤ 1.1× BASELINE; replication delay 99th percentile ≤ 5 s (ASSUMPTION); HL7 acknowledgement time ≤ BASELINE | Load-test report (no patient data) in the migration repository | Committed sizing; whether a one-clinic trial is possible; if it fails, resize or change the setup and re-plan Phase 2 | 1 |\n| V4 | The cloud copy is identical to the live database | Continuous reconciliation per table and partition: counts plus checksums only | Zero unexplained differences for ≥ 14 consecutive days, including a peak Monday and a month-end; clean for the last 72 h before V6 | Reconciliation dashboard export with counts and hashes only, no records | V5 and V6; if it fails, find the cause and the clock restarts; repeated failure flips the replication tool (§3) | Starts in 1, required before 3 |\n| V5 | Cutover and rollback can run without user-visible downtime or data loss | ≥ 2 full rehearsals on a production-sized staging pair across the real circuit (de-identified if the Privacy Officer requires), with injected booking and HL7 traffic; zone-failover test; circuit-cut test | Saving pause ≤ 30 s; zero lost or duplicate bookings against the injected traffic log; zero lost HL7 messages; rollback ≤ 15 min with no data loss; zone and circuit failover with no session loss (all ASSUMPTION, confirmed in Phase 0) | Rehearsal timing logs and integrity reports; versioned runbook | V6; if it fails, fix and rehearse again, or flip to the read-only switchover mode (§3) | 2 |\n| V6 | It is safe to cut over production now | Go/no-go checklist; scripted cutover; predefined rollback triggers | **Go:** V4 clean for 72 h; replication delay < 5 s; window confirmed; staff on site; downtime packs ready. **Approvers:** CIO, CMIO or ambulatory operations director, CAB. **Roll back if:** any integrity difference, or error rate or response time above BASELINE thresholds for 10 min | Signed go/no-go record, cutover log, integrity-check results | Phase 3 soak; if a trigger fires, roll back to on-premises and re-run V5 | 3 |\n| V7 | On-premises can be retired | 30-day soak complete; flow logs on the old hosts; DR restore test; archive restore test | Zero connections to the old hosts for 30 days; second-region restore within the RTO; archive restores; sign-off from the CIO, Privacy Officer and records retention | Flow report, DR test report, restore report, sign-offs | Decommissioning (point of no return); if it fails, keep reverse replication and on-premises running | 4 |\n\n## 7. Cross-cutting concerns\n\n| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | BAA and V1; private network only; hospital-managed keys; skeleton limited to the allow-list | Automated test transactions on the live system for the baseline; tracing on the cloud server; replication-delay alerts; telemetry classified as PHI | Landing zone in Terraform; standard app server image; runbooks in git | Live system untouched; replication turn-off runbook; rollback exercised once |\n| 1 | Vulnerability scans; database access audit to the SIEM; key-rotation schedule | Reconciliation dashboard; alerts on replication delay and HL7 queue depth | Database settings kept as code; load-replay harness versioned | Copies across availability zones; tested backup restore; two diverse circuits |\n| 2 | Penetration test of the cloud app tier; vendor allow-lists pre-staged; access review | Per-consumer view of traffic still on old addresses; rollback-trigger alerts in place | Cutover scripted, the same script for rehearsals and production | Zone and circuit failover tests; paper downtime procedures refreshed |\n| 3 | Fencing (old database read-only, old logins off); emergency access watched during the window | War-room dashboard; integrity checks every 5 min; HL7 message counts in and out | Production cutover runs the exact rehearsed script | Reverse replication; rollback triggers; held HL7 messages released safely |\n| 4 | Media wiped to NIST 800-88; credentials and firewall rules removed | Availability-target alerts on the agreed target; zero-traffic proof for the old hosts | DR region in Terraform; DR runbook | Second-region DR restore tested; backup retention matches policy |\n\n## 8. AI layer\nN/A — no AI component.\n\n## 9. Methodology exceptions\nNone.\n\n## 10. Deliberately deferred\n- **Upgrading the app or database version:** after V7, unless the vendor's end of support forces it sooner.\n- **Re-architecture, or a move to the vendor's own hosted product:** pulled forward after one quarter at steady state, or if the vendor's terms require it.\n- **Moving the interface engine to the cloud:** pulled forward if V3 shows HL7 delay across the link breaks its budget.\n- **Long-term cloud pricing commitments (reserved capacity):** after 60 days of steady usage and against Finance's budget.\n- **Automatic scaling:** pulled forward if the busiest hour gets within 70% of the fixed capacity.\n- **Active-active DR across two regions:** pulled forward if the committed availability or RTO target can't be met by restoring from DR.\n- **Moving the data warehouse and reporting platform:** a separate project once read-only consumers are stable on the cloud copy.\n\n---\n\nThe answers that would change this plan most are:\n1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** Move the hospital's on-premises patient scheduling application and its database to a cloud account the hospital owns. Users, interfaces and outside vendors must keep working throughout.\n- **Type:** Infrastructure plus software. It replaces an existing system (brownfield). It's a large build: protected health information (PHI), clinical users, several teams and vendors, and some decisions that are hard to undo.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness of bookings during the move, then availability, then compliance.\n- **Worst failure:** Two databases accepting writes at once (split-brain), or a cutover or rollback that silently loses or duplicates appointments. Patients miss care or get double-booked, and nobody notices for days. The controls against it are V4, V5, V6 and fencing (only one database can ever accept writes), described in Phase 3.\n\n**Planning assumptions** (if any is false, the plan changes as noted):\n- The hospital runs the system itself on one relational database. The vendor supports running it on cloud servers. Users reach it through hostnames the hospital controls. **If false:** if the vendor's own hosted offering is the target, this becomes a vendor-led move and Phases 1–3 are re-planned around their tools. If desktop clients connect straight to the database, a database-name step is added to Phase 2.\n- **HIPAA applies (US).** If not, V1 is re-scoped to the local rules (for example GDPR or NHS DSPT) and the data-location row in §3 changes.\n- **The scheduling database is not shared with other applications** (for example registration). If it is, the move covers every application on it and Phase 2 grows.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Planned downtime during the move | None visible to users; reading schedules works throughout | REQUIREMENT (the request) | V5, V6 |\n| Pause in saving changes at switchover | ≤ 30 s; in-flight saves are retried, not failed | ASSUMPTION: fits inside normal app and client timeouts. Clinical operations must confirm a pause this short doesn't count as \"downtime\" (Phase 0 task) | V5 |\n| Booking data loss (RPO) | No saved booking lost, through cutover or rollback | ASSUMPTION: a lost booking can mean missed care; Chief Medical Information Officer (CMIO) to confirm | V4, V5 |\n| Time to roll back to on-premises (RTO) | ≤ 15 min | ASSUMPTION: keeps a rollback a short interruption, below the hospital's trigger for paper downtime procedures. Clinical operations to confirm against that trigger | V5 |\n| Speed of key actions (find slot, book, reschedule, cancel) | 95th-percentile time ≤ 1.1× today's | BASELINE measured in Phase 0; the 10% allowance is an ASSUMPTION | V3 |\n| Throughput | Handles 2× today's busiest hour | BASELINE measured in Phase 0; 2× headroom is an ASSUMPTION | V3 |\n| Replication delay (on-premises → cloud) | 99th percentile ≤ 5 s at peak | ASSUMPTION: lets the copy fully catch up inside the 30 s pause | V3, V4 |\n| HL7 interface messages | Zero lost or duplicated | ASSUMPTION: a duplicate scheduling message creates a duplicate appointment in the EHR | V5, V6 |\n| Ongoing availability | — | UNKNOWN: needs the service owner's committed target before Phase 3. The floor is \"no worse than BASELINE\", measured from Phase 0 | Phase 3 soak, Phase 4 |\n| Cloud running cost | — | UNKNOWN: Finance supplies the budget before Phase 1 sizing is committed | Phase 1 exit check, Phase 4 |\n| Running two environments at once | ≤ 90 days from the first patient data in the cloud to decommissioning | ASSUMPTION: one infrastructure team carrying both | Phase 4 |\n\n**Missing inputs, most important first:**\n1. Which product this is, and the vendor's written support and licensing terms for the cloud.\n2. Client type: web, or desktop clients connecting directly to the database.\n3. Database engine, version, size and peak volumes.\n4. Cloud provider, and whether a business associate agreement (BAA, the HIPAA contract with the provider) is already signed.\n5. Clinical operations' definition of \"no downtime\".\n6. Whether the database is shared with other applications.\n\n**Things this plan will not change (each with its cost to change):**\n- Application version: an upgrade means re-testing clinical workflows, which is weeks of work.\n- Database engine: changing it means rewriting the schema and stored code, which is months.\n- HL7 interfaces stay on the on-premises interface engine: re-pointing them affects every partner system.\n- Login stays on Active Directory (AD): changing the login model changes the security boundary.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Any PHI in the cloud (copying the database, the cloud test server) | BAA signed with the cloud provider; V1 | Organizational + security (CONFIRMED under HIPAA) | Exposed (Phase 0) |\n| Turning on replication from the live database; adding the cloud test server | Change advisory board (CAB) approval through the existing change process | Organizational (CONFIRMED) | Deployed (Phase 0) |\n| Full-volume replication, V3 and V4 | Two private circuits on separate paths (carrier lead time of weeks; a VPN is enough for Phase 0) | Organizational + runtime (ASSUMED) | Deployed (Phase 1) |\n| Cloud server sizing and licences | Vendor support statement and licence rights in the cloud; Finance's cost budget | Organizational + economic (ASSUMED) | Committed (Phase 1) |\n| Cloud app servers | AD domain controllers, DNS, time servers, print servers (appointment letters) and email relay reachable from the cloud | Runtime (ASSUMED; found by V2) | Deployed (Phase 1) |\n| Re-pointing consumers; the cutover runbook | V2: the full list of what depends on the system | Validation | Specified (Phase 2) |\n| Cutover thresholds (V5, V6) | Clinical operations' definition of \"no downtime\"; CMIO confirming no booking loss | Decision + organizational | Specified (Phase 0 task, needed by Phase 2) |\n| Outside vendors calling the app (SMS reminders, patient portal) | Their IP allow-list changes and change windows | Organizational (ASSUMED) | Exposed at cutover (Phase 3) |\n| Production cutover | V4, V5, V6; refreshed paper downtime procedures; staff on site | Security + organizational | Exposed (Phase 3) |\n| Decommissioning on-premises | V7; sign-off from records retention and legal | Organizational | Committed (Phase 4) |\n\nAll seven kinds of dependency apply here. The ordinary build dependencies are already covered by the phase order.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates\n\n| Decision | How hard to reverse | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | What would flip it |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Consistency vs availability | R3: a split-brain double-books patients, and that harm can't be undone | One database accepts writes at any moment; no two-way live writing. The switch uses a short pause in saving, with fencing | Users can tolerate a ≤ 30 s pause in saving | V5, V6 | V5 pause exceeds budget → switch over in an app-wide read-only mode with an on-screen banner, in the quietest window |\n| Migration approach | R2: weeks of re-planning | Move the app servers as-is; database on the same engine and version (managed only if it supports native replication; otherwise on a cloud server) | Vendor supports it; no database features block it | Phase 1 compatibility check + vendor statement | Vendor refuses, or a blocking feature turns up → database on a cloud server, same engine |\n| Replication: build vs buy | R2: swapping tools means re-copying the database | Use the database engine's own log-based replication, which also runs in reverse for rollback | Same engine and version on both sides | V4 | V4 finds differences, or native replication is impossible → a third-party change-capture tool with stricter reconciliation |\n| Which system is the official record, and how cutover works | R3: an hour wrong can lose or double bookings | On-premises stays the official record until V6. Then a single database switch, with reverse replication kept running through a 30-day soak | Reverse replication keeps pace | V5, V6 | Any rollback trigger in V6 fires → switch back to on-premises |\n| How consumers find the system | R2: changes coordinated across many teams | Every consumer (users, interfaces, vendors) uses stable hostnames behind a proxy the hospital controls. Cutover becomes a proxy change | Every consumer can be re-pointed | V2 | A consumer can't be re-pointed (hard-coded appliance) → an address-translation shim on-premises |\n| Data-privacy boundary | R3: exposed PHI can't be recalled | PHI only in a hospital-owned account, in-country region, BAA-covered services, private network only, hospital-managed encryption keys. Test environments use de-identified data. Logs and traces that contain identifiers are treated as PHI | Provider covers every service used | V1 | A service isn't BAA-covered, or a data-location rule rules out the region → a different service or region |\n| Network link to the cloud | R2: carrier lead time | Two private circuits on separate paths plus a backup VPN. After cutover, on-site scheduling depends on this link | Failover doesn't drop sessions | V5 (link-cut test) | Failover test fails → add a third path from a different carrier before V6 |\n| High availability and disaster recovery (DR) in the cloud | R2 | Synchronous copies across availability zones in one region. Until V7, the reverse-replicated on-premises copy is the DR. A second-region DR copy is required before decommissioning | Zone failover stays within budget | V5, V7 | Zone failover misses the RTO → re-plan the high-availability setup |\n\n**Low-stakes defaults (R1):** infrastructure code → Terraform; monitoring backend → extend the existing security log system (SIEM) and performance monitoring; build pipeline → the existing one.\n\n**Not applicable:**\n- Monolith vs services: no re-architecture during a move.\n- Sync vs async: inherited (HL7 stays asynchronous through the interface engine).\n- AI rows: no AI component.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\nThe skeleton is the thinnest real path through the new cloud setup, used by IT staff only, with the current system untouched as the fallback.\n\n- **The real request:**\n  1. An IT analyst on the allow-list books, then cancels, a slot for the hospital's designated test patient in a designated test clinic.\n  2. The booking is done through one cloud app server.\n  3. The booking is then read back from the cloud database copy.\n- **Path it takes:**\n  1. Hospital workstation → internal DNS and proxy, on a separate hostname.\n  2. Site-to-site VPN → private-only cloud load balancer → one cloud app server, running the same build as production.\n  3. On-premises live database (still the official record) → interface engine → EHR scheduling message for the test patient.\n  4. Native replication → cloud database copy → a check query confirms the booking arrived.\n- **Deploy, log, monitor, roll back:**\n  - The landing zone and the app server image deploy through the pipeline from Terraform.\n  - Logs and traces go to the SIEM, classified as PHI.\n  - Alerts go to the existing on-call: app health and replication delay.\n  - Rollback: take the server off the hostname, revert the infrastructure code, stop replication through the CAB plan, and destroy the cloud copy's encryption key so the copy can never be read again.\n- **Who can reach it:** only allow-listed IT workstations, on a separate internal hostname. Clinical users keep using the on-premises system unchanged. No outside access. No PHI goes into the cloud until V1 passes.\n- **Exit check (V0):**\n  - The test booking traces end to end through every tier.\n  - One deploy and one rollback run through the pipeline.\n  - A deliberately killed replication stream fires an alert.\n  - First baselines are recorded: speed of key actions, replication delay, and the extra delay of the app calling the database across the VPN. These are a floor at near-zero load, not capacity.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n**Phase 0 — Prerequisites, baselines and the skeleton**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 1.\n- **Depends on:** nothing earlier.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Start the long-lead-time items: CAB approval, BAA, cloud account, order both circuits, ask the vendor for its support and licensing statement, get clinical operations' definition of \"no downtime\" and the CMIO's confirmation on booking loss.\n  2. Measure today's live system through its own change process: automated test transactions for the key actions, the busiest hours, availability.\n  3. Start dependency discovery: network flow logs plus a database connection audit, covering at least 35 days including a month-end (V2).\n  4. Build the landing zone with Terraform: private-only network, hospital-managed keys, SIEM logging, sign-in with multi-factor authentication.\n  5. Pass V1.\n  6. Set up the VPN, seed the cloud database copy, deploy the app server.\n  7. Run V0.\n- **Rollback:** as described in §4. The live system's only change is replication being turned on, which can be turned off under the CAB plan.\n- **Exit check:** V1 and V0 pass; baselines recorded; discovery running.\n\n**Phase 1 — Production-scale data tier and proof the copy is identical**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 2.\n- **Depends on:** V0, V1, both circuits installed.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Compatibility check: vendor statement plus database features in use.\n  2. Size the cloud database and app tier across availability zones.\n  3. Move replication onto the circuits.\n  4. Start continuous reconciliation between the two databases (V4). It compares row counts and checksums only, never records.\n  5. Stand up in the cloud the runtime services discovery found: AD domain controllers, DNS, print servers, email relay.\n  6. Replay production load against the cloud stack (V3).\n  7. Test-restore a cloud backup.\n- **Rollback:** tear down the cloud tier. On-premises is still the official record and still serving everyone.\n- **Exit check:** V3 passes; V4 reconciliation running with alerts; cost estimate checked against Finance's budget.\n\n**Phase 2 — Re-point consumers, cut over read-only consumers first, rehearse**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 3.\n- **Depends on:** V2, V3, V4 running.\n- **Tasks** (smallest exposure first):\n  1. Move every consumer V2 found onto stable hostnames behind the hospital proxy, one consumer group at a time, still pointing at on-premises. Each move is undone with a DNS change.\n  2. Move read-only consumers (data warehouse loads, reports) onto the cloud copy.\n  3. Optional, only if V3 shows the cloud app calling the on-premises database across the link stays within budget: put one low-volume clinic's schedulers on cloud app servers for 1 week.\n  4. Script the cutover runbook.\n  5. Run V5 rehearsals.\n  6. Pre-stage outside vendors' allow-list changes.\n  7. Refresh paper downtime procedures and the printed 48-hour schedules.\n- **Rollback:** re-point each group or read-only consumer back by DNS or proxy.\n- **Exit check:**\n  - V2 and V5 pass.\n  - No traffic on the old addresses for 7 days.\n- **Note on exposure:** the write path can't be trialled with a small group without two databases accepting writes, which §3 rules out. Exposure is narrowed by sequence instead: IT staff, then read-only consumers, then one clinic, then the full switch.\n\n**Phase 3 — Production cutover and soak**\n- **Unlocks:** Phase 4.\n- **Depends on:** V4 (14 days, plus the last 72 h clean), V5, V6.\n- **Tasks**, in the quietest window from the baseline (never just before a release of new booking slots):\n  1. The interface engine holds incoming HL7 messages.\n  2. Pause saving.\n  3. Wait until replication delay is zero.\n  4. Fence: demote the on-premises database to read-only and turn off the old app servers' database logins.\n  5. Promote the cloud database.\n  6. Switch the proxy and drain sessions.\n  7. Release the held HL7 messages.\n  8. Start reverse replication, cloud → on-premises.\n  9. Run booking integrity checks every 5 minutes.\n  10. Soak for 30 days including a month-end.\n- **Rollback:** the same script run in reverse back to on-premises, within the RTO, while reverse replication runs.\n- **Exit check:**\n  - V6 post-cutover criteria held for the whole soak.\n  - Availability at or above BASELINE.\n\n**Phase 4 — Steady state and decommissioning**\n- **Unlocks:** the end of running two environments.\n- **Depends on:** Phase 3 soak; V7.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Build a second-region DR copy and test a restore.\n  2. Make a final archive export and test that it restores.\n  3. Pass V7.\n  4. Stop reverse replication.\n  5. Decommission: wipe media to NIST 800-88, revoke credentials, remove firewall rules.\n- **Point of no return:** stopping reverse replication. V7 guards it.\n- **Exit check:** V7 passes; nothing still depends on the on-premises hosts.\n\n## 6.
